title: Classifying discrete and continuous business variables
scenario_markdown: An operations manager at an e-commerce fulfillment center tracks four business metrics: (1) customer service wait time in minutes, (2) customer complaints logged per shift, (3) outbound shipping package weight in kilograms, and (4) defective items found in a sample of 50 units.
assumptions: Discrete random variables take on countable values (typically integer counts resulting from counting)
Continuous random variables take on any value within an interval (typically resulting from measurement)

approval.notes: Reviewed classification: wait time and package weight are continuous (measured); complaints and defects are discrete (counted integers).

stages.prompt_markdown: How should customer service wait time (measured in minutes) be classified?

options.text_markdown: Continuous, because time can take any value along an unbroken continuum within an interval.
Discrete, because digital stopwatches round time to whole seconds.
options.hint_markdown: Rounding during measurement does not make the underlying variable discrete; time itself is continuous.

options.text_markdown: Categorical, because wait times can be grouped into short, medium, and long.
options.hint_markdown: Grouping quantitative values into bins does not change the numeric nature of the original measurement.

stages.explanation_markdown: Wait time is a continuous random variable because it is a measurement that can take any value within a interval, such as $4.328$ minutes. Any rounding on a clock is a limitation of the instrument, not the variable.

stages.prompt_markdown: How should the number of customer complaints logged during a shift be classified?

options.text_markdown: Discrete, because complaints are countable integer outcomes ($0, 1, 2, \dots$) with no fractional values possible.
Continuous, because the shift complaint count can vary smoothly over time.
options.hint_markdown: A complaint is an indivisible unit; you cannot have $2.7$ customer complaints filed in a single shift.

options.text_markdown: Binary, because each shift either has complaints or does not.
options.hint_markdown: The metric counts the total number of complaints, which can be any non-negative integer ($0, 1, 2, \dots$), not just yes/no.

stages.explanation_markdown: The number of complaints is a discrete random variable because it results from counting distinct, indivisible events. The sample space is $\{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}$.

stages.prompt_markdown: How should outbound shipping package weight (in kilograms) be classified?

options.text_markdown: Continuous, because weight is a physical measurement that can take any real value on a continuous scale.
Discrete, because shipping scales display weight to two decimal places ($0.01$ kg).
options.hint_markdown: Scale display resolution is an instrument limit; true physical mass can take any value in an interval.

options.text_markdown: Ordinal, because heavier packages cost more than lighter packages.
options.hint_markdown: Weight is measured on a continuous ratio scale with meaningful units and ratios, not merely ranks.

stages.explanation_markdown: Package weight is continuous because weight is determined by measurement on a continuum. Between any two possible weights, an infinite number of other weights exist.

stages.prompt_markdown: How should the count of defective items in a sample of 50 inspected units be classified?

options.text_markdown: Discrete, because the possible defect counts are restricted to the finite set of integers $\{0, 1, 2, \dots, 50\}$.
Continuous, because we can compute the sample defect proportion $\hat{p} = X/50$.
options.hint_markdown: The question asks about the count of defective items $X$, which is strictly integer-valued.

options.text_markdown: Continuous uniform, because any unit has equal probability of being defective.
options.hint_markdown: Even if items have identical failure rates, the count of defects is a discrete binomial variable, not a continuous distribution.

stages.explanation_markdown: The number of defective items $X$ in $n = 50$ trials is a discrete random variable (modeled by a binomial distribution) with countable support $\{0, 1, \dots, 50\}$.
